desc:
A single machine must run all jobs, where jobs[i] = [duration, due]. It starts at time 0, runs one job at a time without interruption and without idle gaps, in an order of your choice. If job i finishes at time f, its lateness is max(0, f - due).

Return the smallest possible value of the largest lateness over all jobs (0 means every job can be on time, and also the answer for no jobs).

jobs = [[3, 6], [2, 4]]  ->  0
jobs = [[4, 3], [2, 3]]  ->  3

In the second example, whichever job goes second finishes at time 6 and is 3 late.
hints: Total work is fixed, so the last job always finishes at the same time. The question is which job should be that last one.
Take two neighbouring jobs A then B. If B is due earlier than A, what happens to the maximum lateness of the pair if you swap them?
Run the jobs in increasing order of due time (earliest due date first), then take the largest max(0, finish - due).
editorial: Sort the jobs by due time and simulate. This is the earliest-due-date rule and it is optimal for this objective.

Exchange argument: suppose neighbouring jobs A then B have due(A) > due(B). Let them start at time s. Before the swap the lateness values are s + a - due(A) and s + a + b - due(B). After swapping they are s + b - due(B) and s + a + b - due(A). The second new value is smaller than the old s + a + b - due(B) because due(A) > due(B), and the first new value is smaller than it too. So the maximum of the pair never grows, and repeated swaps reach the sorted order. Time O(n log n).
solution:
def minMaxLateness(jobs):
    t = 0
    worst = 0
    for duration, due in sorted(jobs, key=lambda x: x[1]):
        t += duration
        worst = max(worst, t - due)
    return worst
